did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job opens chapter 13 by claiming that everything his friends know about his situation is not new to him: he has seen, heard, and understood it himself.
Did you know? Job distinguishes his friends’ words from his desire to speak directly with God: he appeals to the Almighty and asks to present his case before Him.
Did you know? Job calls his friends fabricators of lies and worthless physicians—in other words, people trying to fix his situation with false and useless arguments.
Did you know? Job accuses his friends of showing partiality toward God, meaning that they defend God in a biased way instead of honestly examining Job’s situation.
Did you know? Job asks whether God will examine his friends, and warns that they cannot treat God as though He were a person who could be deceived.
Did you know? Job compares his friends’ memories to sayings of ashes and their defenses to clay, images that emphasize the fragility and instability of their arguments.
Did you know? Despite the danger in his words, Job declares that he will not stop speaking and presenting his case before God; this shows his determination to seek a direct hearing.
Did you know? Job says that he has prepared his case and knows that he will be vindicated, expressing his confidence that he has a just claim before God.
Did you know? Before asking to speak with God, Job requests two things: that God remove His hand from him and that His terror not overwhelm him.
Did you know? Job asks how many iniquities and sins are being charged against him, because he does not understand why God hides His face and treats him as an enemy.
